newsitem.title: INDIA: RBI issues credit policy Tuesday- what to watch.
newsitem.headline: RBI issues credit policy Tuesday- what to watch.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announces its monetary and credit policy for the first half of 1997/98 (April-March) on April 15.
The following are bankers and analysts expectations from the credit policy:
* Cut in deposit interest rate cap

Bankers and analysts expect a cut in the maximum interest rate set by the Reserve Bank of India on term deposits with maturity above 30 days and up to one year. Some expect a cut in the interest rate cap to nine per cent per annum from 10.0.

Others expect the introduction of a new slab: 30 days up to six months and above six months up to one year. Interest cap on the first slab would be 8.0 percent and 9.0 on the second. A cut in deposit interest rates would lower banks' cost of funds and enable a cut in lending rates.
* Cut in cash reserve ratio (CRR) on inter-bank borrowings

A long-standing demand in some banking circles, many bankers expect the RBI to announce a removal of CRR on interbank liabilities in the credit policy. Removal of CRR on interbank borrowings would facilitate development of a term money market and the emergence of a reference rate, bankers say.

But in the past, RBI has been against this move. RBI officials say the cost of CRR can be factored into banks' quotes for term money and it need not be an impediment to the development of a term money market.
* Cut in banks' CRR
Some bankers expect a cut in CRR from the present 10 percent. They say it would be in tune with the RBI"s long term goal of reducing CRR to less than 10 percent.
Others say a cut is unlikely, given the current comfortable liquidity levels and banks' difficulty finding borrowers.
* Cut in banks' export credit interest rates

Some bankers expect a cut in banks' export credit rates from 15 percent for credit from 91 days to 180 days and 13 percent for credit up to 90 days. They say a reduction is needed to help exporters, given unsatisfactory exports in 1996/97 (April-March).
Other bankers do not expect any cuts, saying that rates are too low and any cut will make it unattractive for bankers to lend to exporters.
* Increase in banks' limits for investments in shares and debentures

Some bankers expect an increase in limits for bank investments in shares and debentures of companies to 10 percent of incremental deposits from five. A sub-limit may be introduced restricting bank investments to not more than five percent in shares.
Some bankers also expect that such investments may be classified as advances.
* Removal of maximum permissible bank finance (MPBF)
Some bankers expect MPBF to be done away with in the credit policy although most expect only the first steps in a phase-out of the system.
* Foreign investors in debt to be allowed forward cover
One analyst said he expected foreign investors in debt to be allowed to take forward cover. This would safeguard them against exchange risk and make investments in Indian debt more attractive.
* Imposition of reserve requirements on foreign currency deposits and non-resident deposits

Some bankers feel the RBI may impose reserve requirements on such deposits, particulary as it is grappling with the problems of intervention to prevent rupee appreciation against the dollar and consequent sterilisation of rupees entering the monetary system.

Others feel it will not do so as this may be against its long-term policy. Further reintroduction of reserves about a year after they have been scrapped would represent an about-turn in policy and convey a wrong impression about continuity of policies, they say.
* Reintroduction of bridge loans against capital issues
Some bankers expect the RBI to reintroduce bridge loans against forthcoming capital issues. This would help cash-strapped corporates to get projects moving.
--Bombay Newsroom (91) 22 265 9000
